name: Benford's Law (First Digit Distribution)
source: Benford (1938) Proc APS 78:551; Hill (1995) Statistical Science 10:354
notes: Observed first-digit frequencies from Benford's original 20,229 observations across 20 datasets. x = digit, y = observed frequency (%). Multiplicative processes generate logarithmic digit distributions, a hallmark of scale-invariant (power-law family) behaviour.
justification: Benford's law arises from multiplicative random processes and scale invariance. Data spanning multiple orders of magnitude under multiplicative composition yield log-uniform leading digits, placing this squarely in the multiplicative operator class.

name: Pareto Income Distribution (US 2019)
source: US Census Bureau, Current Population Survey 2019; Pareto (1896) Cours d'economie politique
notes: Complementary CDF of US household income. x = income threshold ($k), y = fraction of households above threshold. Upper tail only (top 20%).
justification: Income above the median arises from multiplicative returns (compound growth, leverage, network effects). The Pareto tail is the canonical example of multiplicative wealth accumulation producing power-law distributions.

name: Beer-Lambert Law (Optical Absorption)
source: Beer (1852) Ann Phys Chem; Skoog, West & Holler (2013) Fundamentals of Analytical Chemistry, 9th ed.
notes: Transmittance of 520nm light through CuSO4 solution (0.01 M) vs path length in cm. Each incremental slab removes a constant fraction, an additive contribution to optical depth.
justification: Each additional path-length increment independently absorbs a fixed fraction of remaining intensity. This is additive in the exponent (optical depth = sum of incremental absorptions), producing exponential decay of transmittance.

name: Langmuir Adsorption Isotherm (CO on Pd)
source: Engel (1978) J Chem Phys 69:373; Ertl (2008) Angew Chem Nobel Lecture
notes: Fractional surface coverage of CO on Pd(111) vs CO partial pressure (Torr). Surface sites are finite, producing saturation.
justification: Adsorption sites are a finite resource. Binding is competitive for limited surface area, creating a hard upper bound on coverage. The operator maps input (pressure) through a bounded channel (finite sites), yielding Langmuir/Michaelis-Menten saturation.

name: Monod Growth Kinetics (E. coli on Glucose)
source: Monod (1949) Ann Rev Microbiol 3:371; Kovárová-Kovar & Egli (1998) Microbiol Mol Biol Rev
notes: Specific growth rate (h^-1) vs glucose concentration (mg/L) for E. coli in chemostat. mu_max ~ 0.92 h^-1, Ks ~ 4 mg/L.
justification: Microbial growth rate saturates because cellular enzyme machinery has finite catalytic capacity. Substrate uptake follows Michaelis-Menten kinetics at the transporter level, making the growth-rate response a bounded function of substrate concentration.

name: Ebbinghaus Forgetting Curve
source: Ebbinghaus (1885) Über das Gedächtnis; Murre & Dros (2015) PLOS ONE 10:e0120644
notes: Retention (fraction of nonsense syllables recalled) vs time (hours). Murre & Dros (2015) replicated Ebbinghaus's original experiment.
justification: Memory trace decay is driven by time-additive interference and consolidation failure. Each time interval contributes an independent probability of forgetting, yielding exponential (or near-exponential) decay in retention.

name: Radiocarbon Decay (C-14)
source: Libby (1960) Nobel Lecture; Godwin (1962) Nature 195:984; NIST half-life 5730 ± 40 yr
notes: Fraction of C-14 remaining vs time in thousands of years. t_1/2 = 5730 yr.
justification: Each nucleus has an equal, time-independent probability of decaying per unit time. This constant hazard rate is the defining property of additive-in-time exponential decay.

name: Kepler's Third Law (Solar System Planets)
source: Kepler (1619) Harmonices Mundi; NASA Planetary Fact Sheet (2021)
notes: Orbital period (years) vs semi-major axis (AU) for 8 planets. P^2 = a^3 implies P = a^1.5.
justification: Gravitational orbits arise from the multiplicative interplay of mass and distance in Newton's law. The period-distance relation is a pure power law (exponent 1.5) emerging from scale-free gravitational dynamics.

name: Richardson's Law (Fractal Coastline of Britain)
source: Richardson (1961) General Systems 6:139; Mandelbrot (1967) Science 156:636
notes: Measured length of west coast of Britain (km) vs measurement ruler length (km). Power-law exponent ~1.25.
justification: Coastline measurement is scale-invariant: halving the ruler length reveals self-similar detail at every scale. This multiplicative cascade of detail across scales is the signature of fractal geometry and produces a power-law relationship.

name: Stefan-Boltzmann Radiation (Tungsten Filament)
source: Stefan (1879) Sitzungsber Akad Wiss Wien; Forsythe & Worthing (1925) Astrophys J 61:146
notes: Total radiated power (W/cm^2) vs temperature (K) for tungsten filament. P = epsilon*sigma*T^4.
justification: Thermal radiation intensity is determined by multiplicative scaling of temperature to the fourth power. The Stefan-Boltzmann law is a pure power law arising from the multiplicative structure of Planck radiation integrated over all frequencies.

name: Internet AS Degree Distribution
source: Faloutsos, Faloutsos & Faloutsos (1999) ACM SIGCOMM; CAIDA AS Relationships Dataset
notes: Complementary CDF of autonomous system (AS) node degree. x = degree, y = fraction of nodes with degree >= x. Power-law exponent ~2.2.
justification: Internet topology grows by preferential attachment: highly connected nodes attract disproportionately more connections. This multiplicative rich-get-richer mechanism produces scale-free degree distributions following a power law.

name: Omori's Law (Earthquake Aftershock Decay)
source: Omori (1894) J Coll Sci Imp Univ Tokyo; Utsu (1961); Utsu, Ogata & Matsu'ura (1995) J Phys Earth
notes: Aftershock rate (events/day) vs time after mainshock (days). Data from the 1891 Mino-Owari earthquake. Modified Omori law: n(t) = K/(t+c)^p with p ~ 1.
justification: Aftershock triggering is a cascade process where each aftershock can trigger further aftershocks. This multiplicative branching across scales produces a power-law temporal decay, not exponential.

name: Neural Firing Rate vs Stimulus Intensity
source: Naka & Rushton (1966) J Physiol 185:536; Albrecht & Hamilton (1982) J Neurophysiol
notes: Normalized firing rate of retinal ganglion cells vs light intensity (relative units). Follows Naka-Rushton function R = R_max * I^n / (I^n + sigma^n) with n~2.
justification: Neural firing rate saturates due to refractory periods and finite ion channel availability. The response is bounded above by maximum firing rate and below by spontaneous rate, producing a sigmoidal/Hill-type bounded curve.

name: Photovoltaic I-V Curve (Silicon Cell)
source: Green (1982) Solar Cells; De Soto et al. (2006) Solar Energy 80:78
notes: Current output (A) vs voltage (V) for a standard silicon solar cell under AM1.5 illumination. Current is bounded by photogenerated current I_L.
justification: Photocurrent is bounded by the finite photon flux. As voltage approaches open-circuit, the diode current opposes photocurrent, creating a sharp bounded transition. The system has a hard physical ceiling (I_L) and floor (0).

name: Concrete Compressive Strength vs Age
source: ACI 209R-92; Neville (2011) Properties of Concrete, 5th ed.; Yeh (1998) Cement Concrete Research
notes: Compressive strength (MPa) of ordinary Portland cement concrete vs age (days). Strength gain follows a bounded logarithmic/asymptotic curve approaching ~42 MPa.
justification: Cement hydration consumes finite reactants (unhydrated cement grains). As hydration nears completion, strength gain decelerates toward a hard upper bound set by the water-cement ratio. The process is resource-limited and bounded.

name: Galaxy Luminosity Function (Schechter)
source: Schechter (1976) ApJ 203:297; Blanton et al. (2003) ApJ 592:819 (SDSS)
notes: Number density of galaxies (Mpc^-3 mag^-1) vs luminosity (L/L*). The faint-end slope is a power law with index alpha ~ -1.05.
justification: Galaxy formation involves hierarchical merging, a multiplicative cascade process. The faint-end luminosity function is a power law arising from the scale-free nature of gravitational collapse and merger trees.

name: Sound Attenuation in Air vs Frequency
notes: Atmospheric absorption coefficient (dB/km) vs frequency (Hz) at 20C, 50% RH. Approximately quadratic in frequency (power law exponent ~2).
justification: Sound absorption arises from molecular relaxation processes where energy loss per cycle scales with frequency squared. The relationship is a power law because viscous and thermal losses multiply with the square of the oscillation frequency.

name: Software Defect Density vs Module Size
source: Hatton (1997) IEEE TSE 23:764; Compton & Withrow (1990) CACM 33:169
notes: Defect density (defects per KLOC) vs module size (KLOC). Data from large industrial C and Fortran codebases. Power-law exponent ~0.5.
justification: Software defects arise from combinatorial interactions between code components. As module size grows, the number of potential interaction paths grows multiplicatively, producing a power-law relationship between size and defect density.

name: Protein Folding Kinetics (Two-State, CI2)
source: Jackson & Fersht (1991) Biochemistry 30:10428; Fersht (1999) Structure and Mechanism in Protein Science
notes: Fraction of unfolded CI2 protein remaining vs time (ms) at pH 6.3, 25C. Single-exponential folding with rate constant k ~ 50 s^-1.
justification: Two-state protein folding has a single rate-limiting barrier. The transition from unfolded to folded state is a first-order kinetic process where the probability of crossing the barrier per unit time is constant, yielding exponential decay of the unfolded population.

name: Second-Order Chemical Kinetics (Saponification of Ethyl Acetate)
source: Walker (1906) Proc Royal Soc A 78:157; Atkins & de Paula (2014) Physical Chemistry, 10th ed.
notes: Concentration of ethyl acetate (mol/L) vs time (min) for second-order reaction with NaOH. 1/[A] = 1/[A]_0 + kt, so [A] = [A]_0/(1 + [A]_0*k*t), which is a hyperbolic (power-law family) decay.
justification: In second-order kinetics, the rate depends on the product of two concentrations -- a multiplicative coupling. The resulting 1/[A] vs t linearity is equivalent to a power-law decay [A] ~ t^-1 at long times.

name: Wind Speed Distribution (Weibull, North Sea)
source: Justus et al. (1978) J Appl Meteor 17:350; Hennessey (1977) J Appl Meteor 16:119; KNMI North Sea data
notes: Cumulative distribution function of wind speed (m/s) at IJmuiden, Netherlands. Weibull CDF with k~2.0, lambda~8.5 m/s.
justification: Wind speeds are bounded below by zero and bounded above by finite atmospheric energy. The CDF saturates to 1, and the distribution is shaped by bounded energy dissipation and turbulent mixing, producing a bounded (Weibull) functional form.

name: Dose-Response Curve (Acetylcholine on Frog Rectus)
source: Clark (1926) J Physiol 61:530; Clark (1937) General Pharmacology; Rang (2006) Brit J Pharmacol 147:S9
notes: Fractional contraction of frog rectus abdominis muscle vs acetylcholine concentration (uM). Follows Hill equation with n~1.
justification: Receptor occupancy is bounded by the finite number of receptor molecules. At low concentrations, response is proportional to dose; at high concentrations, all receptors are occupied and the response saturates. This is the defining signature of a bounded operator.

name: Technology Adoption S-Curve (US Electricity Access)
source: EIA Historical Statistics; Grübler (1999) Technological Forecasting and Social Change 56:33; Our World in Data
notes: Percentage of US households with electricity vs year.
justification: Technology adoption is bounded: it cannot exceed 100% of the addressable population. Early adoption accelerates via network effects, then saturates as the remaining non-adopters are harder to reach. The bounded operator (finite market) produces a logistic S-curve.

name: Allometric Brain Mass vs Body Mass (Mammals)
source: Jerison (1973) Evolution of the Brain and Intelligence; Martin (1981) Nature 293:57; Burger et al. (2019)
notes: Brain mass (g) vs body mass (g) for 28 mammal species. Power-law exponent ~ 0.75.
justification: Brain size scales with body size through the same multiplicative vascular-network constraints as metabolic rate. The allometric relationship arises from the fractal branching of nutrient supply networks, producing a power law.

name: River Discharge Flood Frequency (Gumbel)
source: Gumbel (1958) Statistics of Extremes; USGS streamflow data, Mississippi River at St Louis
notes: Annual maximum discharge (1000 m^3/s) vs return period (years). Gumbel extreme-value distribution: x increases exponentially with return period.
justification: Flood peaks arise from the maximum of many independent rainfall events. Extreme value theory shows that the maximum of additive (independent) random variables follows a Gumbel distribution, where the quantile function grows logarithmically (inverse-exponential CDF).

name: Hagen-Poiseuille Flow (Pipe Pressure Drop)
source: Poiseuille (1846) Mém Acad Sci Paris; Sutera & Skalak (1993) Ann Rev Fluid Mech 25:1
notes: Volumetric flow rate (mL/s) vs pipe radius (mm) for water at constant pressure gradient. Q scales as r^4.
justification: Flow rate depends on radius to the fourth power through multiplicative geometric scaling: the cross-sectional area (r^2) multiplied by the velocity profile integral (also r^2). This is a pure power law from multiplicative dimensional analysis.

name: Hubble's Law (Galaxy Recession Velocity)
source: Hubble (1929) PNAS 15:168; Freedman et al. (2001) ApJ 553:47 (HST Key Project)
notes: Recession velocity (km/s) vs distance (Mpc) for nearby galaxies. v = H_0 * d, a power law with exponent 1.
justification: Hubble's law is a linear (power-law exponent 1) relationship arising from the multiplicative expansion of space. Every additional megaparsec multiplies by the same Hubble constant, a scale-free multiplicative process.

name: Population Growth of Yeast (Logistic)
source: Pearl (1927) Q Rev Biol 2:532; Carlson (1913) Biochem Z 57:313
notes: Population density of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (cells x10^6 / mL) vs time (hours) in batch culture. Classic logistic growth with K ~ 13.0.
justification: Yeast growth is bounded by finite nutrients and space. The carrying capacity K is a hard ceiling imposed by resource depletion and waste accumulation. Growth follows a logistic curve: exponential at first, then saturating.

name: Earthquake Magnitude-Frequency (Japan, JMA Catalogue)
source: JMA Seismological Bulletin; Nanjo et al. (2004) GRL 31:L09601
notes: Cumulative number of earthquakes per year with magnitude >= M in Japan (2000-2020). Gutenberg-Richter b-value ~ 0.9. This is a distinct geographical catalogue from domain 10 (global USGS).
justification: The Gutenberg-Richter law is exponential in magnitude because magnitude is itself a logarithmic (additive) transform of energy. Each unit increase in magnitude represents the same additive step in log-energy, and the frequency decreases by a constant factor per step.

name: Planck Radiation Peak Shift (Wien's Displacement Law)
source: Wien (1893) Sitzungsber Preuss Akad Wiss; NIST reference data
notes: Peak wavelength (nm) vs temperature (K). lambda_max * T = 2.898e6 nm*K, so lambda_max = 2.898e6 / T, a power law with exponent -1.
justification: Wien's law is a pure inverse power law (exponent -1) arising from the multiplicative scaling symmetry of the Planck spectrum. Doubling temperature halves the peak wavelength -- scale-free multiplicative behaviour.

name: Atmospheric Pressure vs Altitude
source: US Standard Atmosphere (1976); NOAA/NASA
notes: Pressure (hPa) vs altitude (km) in the troposphere and lower stratosphere. Each equal altitude increment removes a constant fraction of remaining atmosphere.
justification: In an isothermal atmosphere, each thin layer supports the weight of all layers above it. The pressure decrement at each layer is proportional to the current pressure -- a constant-rate additive process in altitude yielding exponential decay.

name: Michaelis-Menten Enzyme Kinetics (Lactase)
source: Wallenfels & Malhotra (1961) Adv Carbohydr Chem 16:239; Kim & Gadd (2008) Enzyme Microb Technol
notes: Rate of lactose hydrolysis (umol/min/mg) by beta-galactosidase vs lactose concentration (mM). V_max ~ 550, K_m ~ 1.5 mM.
justification: Enzyme active sites are finite. At low substrate, rate increases linearly; at high substrate, all active sites are occupied and the rate plateaus at V_max. The bounded operator (finite catalytic sites) produces Michaelis-Menten saturation.

name: City Rank-Size Distribution (World Cities)
source: Gabaix (1999) QJE 114:739; UN World Urbanization Prospects (2018)
notes: Population of world's largest cities vs rank. Zipf's law for cities: population ~ rank^(-1).
justification: City sizes arise from multiplicative growth processes (proportional growth, Gibrat's law). Cities that are already large attract more migrants and investment at rates proportional to their current size, producing a scale-free power-law rank-size distribution.

name: Capacitor Charging (RC Circuit)
source: Horowitz & Hill (2015) The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed.; standard RC circuit
notes: Voltage across capacitor (V) vs time (ms) for 10V source, R=1kOhm, C=1uF. V(t) = V_0(1 - exp(-t/RC)). Bounded by supply voltage.
justification: The capacitor voltage is bounded by the supply voltage. As the capacitor charges, the current decreases because the voltage difference driving it shrinks. The system asymptotically approaches the supply rail -- a textbook bounded process.

name: Newton's Law of Cooling
source: Newton (1701) Phil Trans; Vollmer (2009) Eur J Phys 30:1063
notes: Temperature excess above ambient (K) vs time (min) for a cooling cup of coffee. T_ambient = 22C, T_0 = 90C.
justification: The rate of heat loss is proportional to the current temperature difference. This constant proportional rate per unit time is the hallmark of additive-in-time exponential decay.

name: Zipf's Law for Web Page Popularity
source: Breslau et al. (1999) IEEE INFOCOM; Adamic & Huberman (2002) Glottometrics 3:143
notes: Number of requests vs rank for web proxy cache traces. Power-law exponent ~ 0.7-0.8.
justification: Web popularity follows preferential attachment: popular pages attract more links and clicks in proportion to their current popularity. This multiplicative feedback produces a power-law rank distribution, distinct from the word-frequency Zipf domain (id 6).

name: Haemoglobin-CO2 Dissociation (Bohr Effect)
source: Roughton (1964) Handbook of Physiology; Kelman (1966) J Appl Physiol 21:1375
notes: CO2 content of blood (mL CO2 / 100 mL blood) vs pCO2 (mmHg). Bounded by finite haemoglobin binding capacity and plasma solubility.
justification: CO2 binding to haemoglobin saturates because binding sites are finite. The total CO2 content combines dissolved CO2 (linear) with bound forms (saturating), producing a bounded curve approaching a maximum carrying capacity.

name: Diffusion-Limited Aggregation (Cluster Radius vs Mass)
source: Witten & Sander (1981) PRL 47:1400; Meakin (1983) Phys Rev A 27:1495
notes: Radius of gyration vs number of particles in DLA cluster. R ~ N^(1/d_f) with fractal dimension d_f ~ 1.71 in 2D, so exponent ~ 0.58.
justification: DLA clusters are self-similar fractals. The radius-mass relationship is a power law because the structure is scale-invariant: zooming in or out reveals statistically identical branching patterns. This is a multiplicative cascade of spatial structure.

name: Thermal Conductivity of Copper vs Temperature
source: Touloukian et al. (1970) Thermophysical Properties of Matter, Vol 1; Ho et al. (1972) J Phys Chem Ref Data 1:279
notes: Thermal conductivity of OFHC copper (W/m/K) vs temperature (K). Shows rise to a peak near 20K then decrease, but the high-T branch (>50K) shows bounded power-law decrease toward a plateau near room temperature. Here we use the 50-1000K regime where conductivity approaches a bounded asymptote.
justification: At elevated temperatures, phonon-phonon scattering dominates and thermal conductivity approaches a finite lower bound. The conductivity is bounded below by the minimum mean free path (Ioffe-Regel limit) and above by the low-temperature peak, producing bounded behaviour.

name: World Population Growth (Logistic Fit, 1800-2100)
source: UN DESA World Population Prospects (2022); Maddison Project Database (2020); Kapitsa (1996) Phys Usp
notes: World population (billions) vs year. Historical data 1800-2020, UN medium projection to 2100. Logistic carrying capacity ~11 billion.
justification: Global population is bounded by finite planetary resources, arable land, and energy. After exponential growth in the 19th-20th centuries, growth rates have declined as the system approaches carrying capacity. This is a textbook logistic (bounded) process.
